EXPLOSION AND LOSS OF LIFE ON BOARD THE FRENCH ROYAL YACllT. A frightful accident occurred on Monday, on board tiie royal screw propeller yacht « Gomte d'Eu." She had left Havre in the morning for Cherbourg, wlieie some of her fittings were to have been completed, nnd she was to proceed thence to Trepoit, to take on hoard his Majesty Louis Phillippe, and part of the royal family, for a pleasure excursion. The steamer was going at its usual speed when about noon, a mass of steam was seen to escape from all the outlets of the engine room. The first moment of panic being passed, gangs were speedily formed for the purpose of throw ing cold w ater into the engine room. The heat of t he steam, even on deck, was so great, that it was almost impossible to move about in it ; and i' was known that 20 engineers and firemen were in the greatest danger near the furnaces. Three of them soon eniergr d froni the hatches, and fell senseless on deck. Before ten o'clock in the evening nine had expired The steamei's head had meanwhile been turned toward Jiavre, she being then near Barfieur. When the steam had suflicieu'ly escaped to allow the examination of the engine it was discovered that the boiler had hurst in the under part, corresponding with the furnaces ) and the boiling water falling upon the fite, and running through the grates, had deluged with its burning waves the whole of the engine room. the effect upon the unforiu nate men who were at that time in the tengine-room must have been immediate, and instant suffocation must have been the fate of the persons who were nearest the boilers þÿ The " Oointe d'Eu" arrived in the roads of Havre at two o'clock in the morning of Tuesday, when ihe killed and wounded were placed in boats, and brought on shore Of the immediate survivors, eleven in number, who had been sent to the hospital, four expired on Tuesday, and there is little hope enlettaincd pi the ultimate recently ot the remainder. In the temperate climates of the old world, there is great uniformity in the gradual progress of men from the savage stale to the highest civilization ; beginning with hunting and fishing, advancing to flocks and herds, and then to agriculture and commerce. One will he much disappointed, if he expect the same progress in America. Among the northern tribes, there is nothing that resembles the shepherd state : they continue hunters and fishers as originally ; because there is no cause so potent as to force them from that slate to become shepherds. So far clear. But there is another fact of which we have no example in the old world, that seems not so easily explained: these people, without passing through the shepherd state, have advanced to some degree of agriculture. Before the seventeenth century, the Iroquois or Five Nations had villages, and cultivated Indian corn : the Cherokecs have many small towns ; they raise corn in abundance, and enclose their fields : they breed poultry, and have orchards of peach trees. The (Jhickesaws and Creek Indians live pretty much in tiie same manner. The Apalachiles sow and reap in common ; and put up tiie corn in granaries, to be distributed among individuals when they want food. The Hurons raise great quantities of corn, not only for their own use, but for commerce. Many of these nations, particularly the Cherokecs, h ive of late got horses, swine, and tame (tattle; an improvement borrowed from the Europeans. But coru isolan earlier date; when Sir

Richard Greenville tr»> >k possession of Virginia in the reign of Queen Elizabeth, the natives had corn; and Hennepin assures us, that the nations bordering on the Mississippi had corn long before they were visited by an European. Husbandry, it is Hue, is among those people still in its infancy ; being lelt to the women, who sow, who leap, who shoe up in public granaries, and who distribute as need requires The inhabitants ol Guiana in South America, continue to this day hunters and fishers. But though they have neither flocks nor herds, they have some husbandry ; for the women plant cassava, yams, and plantains. They make a liquor like our ale, t tnned piworee, which they drink with their food And tho they aie exlieinely loud of that liquor, their indolence makes them otien neglect to provide against the want of it. To a people having a violent propensity to intemperance, as all savages have, this improvidence is a blessing ; lor otherwise tin v would wallow in perpetual drunkenness They are by no means singular ; lor unconcern about futurity Is tho characteristic of all savages; to forego an immediate lor a distant enjoyment, can only be suggested by cultivated reason. When the Canary islands were fust visited by Europeans, which was in the fourteenth century the inhabitants bad coin; lor which tiie ground was prepared in tho following manner. They had a wooden ins! i ument, not unlike a hoe, with a spur or tooth at the end, on which vvas fixed a gout's horn. With this instiumeui the ground was

Btiircd; and if ruin came not in its proper season, water was brought by canals from the rivulets. It was the þÿwomen s province to reap the corn: they took only the ears; which they threshed with slicks, <>i heal with their feet, and then winnowed in their hands Husbandry probably will remain in that state among American savages; lor as they are decreasing daily, they can have no difficulty 1,1, mil food. The lact however is singular, of a people using corn before tame cattle: there must b : a cause, which on better acquaintance with that people will probably be discovered.

SHADDOCK-TliEE. The shaddock ts a native ol Chinn, and the neighboui ing countries, where the name of þÿ sweet þÿball is given to it. Its common name is derived from Captain Shaddock, who brought it ftom Chinn to the West Indies. It has, however, been neglected there, and is now hut seldom entitled to its oriental name of sweet ball. Instead of propagating the shaddock by budding, as is done in China, and which is the only way it can he improved, or even kept from degenerating, they have reared it from seed, and have iri consequence only obtained a harsh arid sour sou of little value. The shaddock came to England from the West Indies, and was cultivated by Miller in 1733. In the West it is certainly the least valuable of the genus to which it belongs : and for the attention which it has received it is chiefly indebted to the showiness both of the tree and the fruit. In its native country the fruit attains a much greater size than in the West. Thunberg says that it is commonly of the size of a þÿchild s head it; Japan; Dr. Sickler describes it as weighing fourteen pounds, and as having a diameter of from seven to eight inches þÿ Their accounts are confirmed by Bishop Heber, who thus describes the shaddock of India : þÿ þÿ The shaddock resembles a melon externally, but it is in fact a vast orange, with a rind of two inches thick, the pulp much less juicy than a common orange, and with rather a bitter flavour, certainly a fruit which would be little valued in England, but
which in this burning weather I thought rather pleasant and þÿrefreshing. The shaddock has been recently sold in London uuder the name of þÿ forbidden þÿftuit,

America þÿ In beholding this fine young giant of a world, with all its magnificent capabilities greatness, I think every Eng- for lishman must feel unmingled regret at the unjust and unwise course of policy which alienated such a child from the paienl government. But at the same time it is impossible to avoid seeing that some other course must, ere long, have led to the same result, even if England had pursued a more maternal course of conduct towards America. No one, beholding this enormous country, stretching from ocean to ocean, watered with ten thousand glorious rivers, combining every variety of climate and soil, therefore every variety ol produce and population; possessing within itself every resource that other nations are forced either to buy abroad, or to create substitutes for at home ; no one, seeing the internal wealth of America, the abundant fertility of the þÿearth surface, s the riches heaped below it, the unparalleled facilities tor the intercourse of men, and the interchange of their possessions throughout its vast extent, can for an instant indulge the thought that such a country was ever destined to he an appendage to any other in the world, or that any chain of circumstances whatever could have long mainiau ed independence a people furnished with every means of freedom and greatness. But Iar from regi citing that America has thrown off her allegiance, and regarding her as a rebellious subject, and irreverent child, England will surely, ere long, learn to look upon this

country as the inheritor of her glory ; the young England destined to perpetuate the language, the memory, the virtues of the noble land from which she is descended. þÿ Loving and honouring my country as I do, I cannot look upon Ameiica will) any feeling of hostility. 1 not only hear the voice of England in the language of this people, but I recognise in all their best qualities, their industry, their honesty, 'heir sturdy independence ol spirit, the very witnesses of their origin þÿ they are English; no other people in the world would have licked us as they did ; nor any other people in the world, built up, upon the ground they won, so sound, and strong, and lair an edifice. þÿ Mrs. butler's Journal.

THE ROMANCE OF ROBBERY. A German collection of remarkable trials has just been published, which contains some extraordinary cases of successful fraud. '1 he first of these is that of a native of Beilin, of low extraction, named Grosjean ; who, under the assumed name of Carl Grandison, made splendid figures in several parts of Germany, appearing at intervals throughout a period of twelve j /ears as a wealthy merchant ti a v riling with his family tor pleasure. At Hoidclhurg especially, and in the neighboui hood of that city, lie twice resided lot a length of
3 IF.

time, on each occasion with his wile and þÿfamily -an object of general esteem and admiration. His establishment was of the richest kind ; his entertainments were noble and frequent; his manners, efccept for a certain tendency to boasting, were thought to be in the highest degree winning and delightful. Tire public regard acquired by a prosperous air and social disposition was enhanced bv the domestic virtues and admirable conduct of his very handsome wife She seemed to he a pattern of þÿpropriety cheerful and amiable when in company, but greatly preferring retirement, in which she devoted herself with exemplary þÿcare especially during the fre qoent absence of her husband on short business journeys to the education of two þÿ lovely and well Conducted children. After tins happy family had lived for some time at Heidelburg, universally popular and adini ted, in 1802 some questionable circumstances look place in connection with the members of a family that had become Ultimate with the Grandissons, in which an unaccountable 1 "ss of money came to Ire talked of, with some other strange transactions ; but all in a manner that appeared to reflect chiefly on one of the young men of ihat family, w ho had fallen, as it seemed, hopelessly in love with the merchant's beautiful wife. The matter came to no certain conclusion: the youth fled, and ihe Grandissons left Heidelburg in consequent of the disgust which this occurrence had caused. Eight years later they re appeared there, with the -same splendid

equipage, and living in itie same admirable manner. This second sojourn lasted for three years ! when a mere accident led to the discovery of the facts which rendered the case surprising. The wealth of Grandisson w is the fruit of a regular plunder of the pub lie mails, which without any accomplice in the act, he had systematically cauied on for years with entire impunity. His short ah- Settees were employed on expeditions of tins kitid : during which he must have committed almost countless robberies of large sums of money and other valuables, without detection in a single instance, returning to the bosom of his family with the plunder which he had collected The discovery was brought about during one of these absences, by a letter, intended to extort money, Irom one who had accidentally found out some of his minor speculations, and tiad traced the offender at last to Ins abode. It then became apparent that Ihe whole life of this flourishing person had been a series of every kind of theft. While the wealth gained by his larger felonies was expended in keeping up a stately appearance, he could not repress t lie petty desire of stealing any trifle that fell in his way in shops, dwelling houses, nay, in the very place where he lived on 'the footing of a grand personage. Yet at this time not a suspicion was raised, until the detection of his greater robberies had come to pass. The condition and history of the wife are hardlv less curious than this long success ol a wholesale system of plunder, combined with Ihe

incessant practice of the meanest pilfering. JSfie appears to have been at once conscious of her þÿhusband s iniquities, studious to conceal them, wavering between fits of abandoned conduct and long intervals of domestic propriety þÿ fort, on the wide, sick of the deception she was made to practice, and Sincerely desirous to give a virtuous edtion lion to her children. Both husband and wife weie mere adventureis at ihe outset. The

5 31 t> 3 2 3 man began his course of crime, when a valet, by robbing his master; and soon afterwards entered upon a career of pretences, treacheries. and felonies, on the grandest as well as on the smallest scale þÿ so dexterously planned and so long undetected, that the story of them sounds a more like a romance than a reality of the nineteenth century. To complete the tale, it may be added that the culprit, when apprehended at Berlin, escaped punishment by committing suicide, in a man ner showing desperate resolution, belore his examination could take place. þÿ London Mercury.

At this moment, the car broke under its superincumbent weight, and Emperor, represented by a waiter ol a coffeehouse who was remarkable for his supposed resemblance to Napoleon, and who was invested with the well known threecornered hat and green uniform, came headlong to the spot Horn which he hud risen, in the terrified sittln of upwards of 10,000 spectators. To Obtain Heights which cannot be Measured. þÿ In reply to an iuquiier, who asks how he can obtain the height of a tower without measuring it t þÿ 'l ake any two rods of unequal length ; place the short rod at any convenient distance from the building, and the long rod at such a distance frotn it, that looking over the short rod to the top of the building, the top of the long rod shall cut that sight. Then say, as the distance lietween the rods is to the height of the long rod over the short one, so is the distance of the long rod from the building to the height of the building, to which result add the short rod, and you have the height ol the building. The corporation 6f Liverpool having recently paved the courts and alleys of that town, it has been observed that the health of the people residing in them has wonderfully improved, and that deaths were less frequent. This led to farther inquiry, and attention was directed to six of the worst courts in Liverpool. Of them Mr. Carr, of the southern dispensary, remarks that they were formerly so notoriously unhealthy that the medical attendant was hardly ever out of them, aud when any epidemic visited the town these places exhibited their results in perfection ; the surface being in a most disgraceful state, covered to some depth with putrid mud, so that the inhabitants were compelled to place large stones at intervals to enable them to reach their houses by stepping from one to another. It is also stated by Mr. Samuel Holme that in þÿFreemason r s ow he found about two years ago a court of houses, the floors of which wore below the public street, and the area of the whole court wns a floating mass of ptitri fled animal and vegetable matter, so dreadfully offensive that lie was obliged to make a

precipitate retreat; yet the whole of the houses were inhabited. Since these sinks of insalubrity have been paved the change in the health of the inhabitants lias been more remarkable than what may have be<Ai anticipated. In one place, (Idridport court.) which contains eighteen houses, the cases of sickness were eighteen before to four after the flags were laid down, lo another alley (Oak court) the proportion is five cases now to twenty eight in former years; and So far as observation has been extended, which it has been to fifty seven of the houses, the fronts of which have been paved, to eighty five cases of sickness which oeemred before paving, only sixteen have taken place since. The obvious effect of smoothing causeways, by means of flags or other paving materials, is to do away with such inequalities as form receptacles for the stagnant water left by rain, and the offals of food with which the poor are apt to strew the fronts of their residences. The malaria thus produced is productive of agues and other painful and fatal diseases. It is there fore the duty of all official persons who have the charge of these matters in towns, not only to see that their streets are well paved for the convenience of pedestrians, but for the health of the public þÿ Chamber's Ldin. burgh Journal.

Mr. Morrison took the bet, and gave him for the text. 4 And the ass opened his mouth and he þÿspake. On another occasion Morrison enlreated an officer to pardon a poor soldier foi some offence he had committed. Every arrival horn tlm West Indies brings us accounts concerning the ugilation in those islands under the II iiish dominion, growing out of (he recent sugar laws of the Imperial Parliament. The repeal ot the old sugar laws has given great oHence to the colonists. These laws gave them a complete monopoly in the British market, by imposing a higher duty on slave grown sugar than upou sugar grown where slavery was abolished. Meet ings have been held throughout the whole island, and leagues have been formed, having lor their object the agitation of the question, and ih; p eseniuti n to the British Parliament of memorials urging the lepeal of the new and the re-enactment of the old sugar law. In this þÿday s paper we have given upon tins subject a great deal ot intelligence hum several islands, which has been received at tins otiice. h will he remaiked, however, that all these proceedings are founded upon a full acknowledgment of the superiority of the British rule, and that there is no immediate appear, ance of any inclination to constitute them selves iuto a republic, or to throw oil the s ivereigniv of the British government. No doubt there are many individuals ii: the West Indies, as well as in (Juba and Canada, who are looking forward to the ddv when all these dependencies will tie severed Irorn iheir present connection With Europe ; but it is a great exaggeration of the truth to represent that there is artv great excitement in any of these islands oi dependencies, having for its

object the immediate establishment of a iepublican form of government. We ought not to deceive ourselves by the representstions of visionary enthusiasts, or he led away by ridiculous statements circulated through ignorant sources Tire people ol lire West India Islands have been, it is true, neglected very much by the Biitish Parliament, and their interests have been sacrificed by the policy it has pursued towards them ; hill it does not appear that there is any seiious intention formed, at the present lime, to cast off all dependence upon the mother country, where, under the old sugar laws, they had the beat market for their productions that vea3 to be bad in lire whole commercial World. Indeed, according to recent intelligence relating to the plans and movements in Downing street, it seems that the British Ministry are contemplating the astonishing plan of making the foreign colonies separate independencies, and of giving to each of them n branch of the royal family as a Viceroy, as Louis Philippe has given Algeria þÿ by this means having in view both the dividing the royal expenses among them, and of saving the colonies in fact. Queen Victoria is a fine, healthy, prolific, child-beat ing young woman; and has already produced five princes and princesses Prince Albert too, is a good looking, substantial, gentlemanly youih, and might he the father of twenty more princed or princesses before his hair begins lo turn grey. þÿ Now, the addition lo the royal family of twelve or fifteen younger branches

is a serious thing to the treasury of England, as it has already been found, by the increased expenditure caused by the four or live rovill children which exist already. At this moment the government is obliged to cltSfld

and enlarge and build more apartments id Buckingham Palace, for the accommodation of ihe royal children. It is, therefoie, now seriously contemplated by the British Ministry to provide for the royal and increasing face, by setting apart Canada for one. the West Indies for another, a part of the East Indies for another, and so on, olher dependencies for other members ol the royal family as they may arise. Thus they will send out their princes from England, in order to get fid of them, and make the colonies support their part of the royal burthens. This plan is seriously contemplated in England; but if it ever will he carried out, is rather problematical. At all events, Canada, the West Indies, and oilier interesting Countries, are making no immediate movement or agitation for slinking ofl the dominion of England or establishing a republic. All that has been seen about such things in newspapers, is much like " Bubble, bubble, Toil and tiouble " Whenever they are ready for touch a movement, they will act, and not before.

We subjoin the following from the Journal de St. Petersburg, of the 23d ult , which will give our readers (if it is considered that the citadel there is only one of the places of deposit established by the gnvernu en') an idea of the immense quantity of precious metals which the Emperor ol Russia has at his command : þÿ þÿ St Petersburg, Oct 23d. þÿ Gold and silver having again been collected in the Imperial Exchequer (to the amount of 8,678,- 569 rubles 20 copeks silver), it was tesoived that tins tr a u e should be deposited in tlie citadel here. After the above-mentioned sum had been duly veiified in the presence o( the proper officers þÿ namely, Privy Councillor Briscorn, the Members ot the Privy Council, and the Deputies of the Exchange, it was carried in the usual form and with a military escort to the citadel of St Peter and St. Paul. And there, after another verification had taken place in the presence of Prince Peter of Oldenburg, and the Commandant of the citadel, General Skotielevv, and a formal document having been drawn up and signed by all the individuals present, it was deposited in the vaults appropriated for that purpose. The whole quantity deposited in this vault alone now amounts to 115,678.595 rubles 19 copeks of þÿsilver. 'Pile silver ruble is equal lo 3s. 2d, English money ; the amount of specie, therefore, in the citadel of S'. Petersburg!! alone is more than eighteen millions and a quarter sterling !

THE ROTARY STEAM EM WE. Mr. Elijah Galloway has just brought,, to perfection a true rotary steam-engine, a most important improvement upon its predecessors. The engine has been tested at the workshop of the Great Western Railway at Paddington, and is now at work at Mr. þÿTyrreli sfactory. Deptford, driving a fan blower, it is between lour and five horse power, and the whole of the machinery is contained in a circular box of about 1 foot in diameter, and weighing about 2j cwt. It ts impossible to explain it satisfactorily without drawings, but it may be described as consisting segments of of circles, so arinuged that the abutment and pistons, or acting arms, bear on each other, so as to secure steamtight contact without any packing. The moving power proceeds directly from the centre of this box to the vis inertia to be acted upon, whether it bo screw, paddle, or locomotive driving wheel, or drum. Its simplicity, and the almost impossibility of its g tting out of order, are not among its least advantages. The patantees assert for it that it is perfectly steam-tight þÿ that its motion and power are uniform at all velocities, and with no perceptible wear or friction ; that it has what engineers will understand by the term þÿ no d ead þÿpoint; and that it works full power up to the size required. So impressed are the authorities at the Admiralty with the importance ol the invention that Captain Fitzmaurice has been directed to send in an estimate lor fitting the Minx with

an auxiliary screw propeller, worked by one ol these rotary engines of 50 horse power. þÿ The Minx is a sailing vessel of about 300 tons burden, and we understand that the saving in weight of machinery alone, by adopting the rotary steam engine, will be at least 50 tons. The ordinary machinery would occupy a space of about 30 square feet, while the machinery of þÿGalloway ert- s t'lnc may ho comprised in a box somewhat less in si-.e than a þÿseaman s chest ! ST< C ATI 3% Disinfection. þÿ Mr. Ellerman, formerly Hanoverian consul at Antwerp, fias recently announced that, in conjunction with M. Dam, of Brussels, and M. Coularet, ot Paris, lie has discovered a process by which the offensive and poisonous exhalations aiising Irom drains, cesspools, privies, slaughter houses, <fcc., may be disinfected in a tew minutes, and rendered almost inodorous, and the matter atierwards converted into a valuable manure, which may be used either in a liquid or pulverised state. If Mr. þÿEllerman s anticipations be realised, and that the re agent which lie applies be found practically available, he will no doubt have conferred a most valuable boon upon society. He says in bis pamphlet : þÿ Bv adopting the process which I wish to introduce as an immediate and permanent disinfectant, the lives of thousands may be spared, and a vast quantity ol human misery be avoided. Unhealthy places will be rendered salubrious, and agi icuiturists wiil derive an immense benefit Irom die rich manure that henceforward can be manufactured even in the centre ol densely populated cities, without creating die least odour or inconvenience, and all that valuable matter which is now shamefully lost will become a Source of great profit and benefit to soe.ieiv. During the decomposition ol feculent matter, the azole changes into ammonia, and the sulphur into sulphuretted hydrogen Scientific men are well aware of the pernicious effects produced by ibis deleterious gas, which blackens metals and changes the colour of

paint and gildings. By die application of my process, the disinfection is instantaneous and permanent, and both liquid and solid matter, as well as the contents of drains, die blood and dung of animals, <kc.., are rendered perfectly inodorous. The disinfection is produced by the application ot a chemical reaclive, varying from one to three per cent., possessing ihe pmperly of neutiulising infectious gases by turning them into sails, which remain in suspension, thus adding their quota to the fertilising qualities ol the þÿmanure. þÿ We were on Tuesday invited to witness some experiments at Grove lane Hackney, at which seveial members ol the board of guardians and the medical gentlemen of Ihe district were present. Mr. Ellermaf) applied Ins re agent to night soil, from which the most offensive effluvium exhaled, and in a few minutes the smell was completely removed. A gentleman, named Redwood, connected wiih the Pharmaceutical Society, proposed to test the efficacy ol the disinfectant by submitting to its action some chemical compounds with which he had come provided; and, after some demur, Mr. Ellerman consented. A portion of phosphurel of of calcium was added to the þÿ villanous com þÿpound, and a cloud of most offensive vapour, mingled with bright flames, rose from the soil : the application of the re agent very soon overcame the peculiar smell, and a similar result took place with the hi-sulphuret of carbon, a still more pungent and penetrating odour which is given oui in the decom-

position of animal matter The gentlemen present expressed themselves perfectly salis. lied with the experiments. Mr Ellerman applies his disinfecting fluid in the propoition ot from one lo three per cent, of the mailer to be operated upon So far as destroying the offensive effluvium of animal matter, the re-agent was quite succcs-fol ; of its application for agricultural purposes wc have no means ol judging, and it i cumins yet lo be

ascertained whether by removing the odour of decomposing animal and vegetable matter we get rid of the peculiar pimciple by which infection is disseminated in ciowded, illdrained, and ill- ventilated localities. þÿ Morn, ing Herald.

(COA1A1 YJ me AT ED) North Side Estate, October 20th 1847. To the Planters of Santa Croix. Gentlemen, In my letter of the 6th Inst., signed a þÿPlanter and which appeared in this Journal of last Thursday 1 staled to you my intention of addressing you a series of letters on subjects connected with planting. Among those subjects, there are none perhaps of more importance than Tillage. This then I have selected lor consideration on the piesent occasion. Tillage, as we all understand the term, is a mechanical division of the soil; but the degree of pulverization soils should receive ; the season, at which it should be given, the number of times the process of pulverizing should be repeated ; the depth to which the plough, hoe, &c., should be made to go, with the reasons for all these things are points with which it is presumed all are not equally familiar. The amount of Tillage that the soil should receive both before and after planting, and during the growth of the plant whether young or old, that is to say whether plant or ratoon cane, de| ends in some measure upon circumstances If the soil be of a friable nature or very light, with little depth, much expense and labour will be thrown away by fiequent sliring of the ground, or if the land be mountainous or hilly the expense of much pulverizing may be greater than the advantages expected to be realized, but with regard to all deep, stiff or adhesive soils, or soils even moderately so the most economical, and at the same time, the most efficacious means of increasing their

richness and fertility is by a judicious mode of tillage ; ot which, considering tire quantity of land each Planter lias in occupation, and the agricultural force at his command too much cannot be given, and the more argillaceous or clayey or stiff the soil is provided draining is not necessary, arid the more ploughing, hoeing &c., (and the deeper the better) is required. The reasonableness of these statements will appear in the following observations: þÿ matter is susceptive of infinite divisibility, and being so, it is evident that the more you divide a clod, the greater the surface you present to external influences, viz : þÿ the rays of the sun ; the atmosphere, the dew, electricity and the like ; the elements of which are continually acting upon every substance, or medium into which r hey are admitted, creating chemical chai ges, which the enlightened of most countries know now full well how to torn to profitable account. Hut when the cultivator of the soil fails to avail himsell of the said influences by not subjecting his lands to them, to the extent they may be subjected, those agents of productiveness are of little use to him. and he pays the penalty of his want of information or exertions in deficient crops, connected closely with the subject is the fact that Tillage by bringing from the depth in the ground to which your implements of husbandry go, all the particles of the tilled land within the sphere of such influences, lias a similar effect to manure, with this differ-

ence only that while the former acts mechanically the latter operates chemically ; for the elements ol manure combining with those of the soil, produce fermentation, which is nothing more than the atoms composing one substance separating by the repulsive force of heat and by chemical attraction, to unite themselves with the atoms of another substance tor which they have a gi eater affinity. Having exceeded the limits a letter prescribes, 1 must reserve what remains to be said on þÿ this part of ihe subject to another opportunity. In the meanwhile, 1 remain. Gentlemen, very respectfully yours, // .4 SMITH

No Deformity in Nature. þÿ f hold that there is a general beauty in the works of Gml, and therefore no deformity in any kind of species of creature whatsoever. 1 cannot tell by what logic we call a toad, a bear, or an elephant ugly, they being created in those outward shapes and figures which best expiess the actions of their inward forms And having past that general visitation of God, who saw that all that he had made was good, that is, conformable to his will, which abbots deformity, and is the rule of order and beauty. 1 here is no deformity but in monstrosity, wherein, notwithstanding, there is a kind of beauty ; Nature so ingenious y contriving the irregular parts as they became sometimes more remarkable tiian ilte principal fabiic þÿ Po speak vet more narrowly, there was » never anything ugly or misshapen, but the chaos ; wherein, notwithstanding, to speak strictly there was no deformity, because no form, nor was it yet impregnant by the voice of God. Now Nature is not at variance with \it, nor Art with Nature, they being bo:h servants of his providence. Art is the pet lection of Nature. Were the world now as it was on the sixth day, there were vet a clems Nature hath made one world and Art another, in brief, all tilings aie artificial ; for Nature is the Art of God. þÿ Sir Thomas Brown's Heligio Medici.

A very severe shock of earthquake was fell in this place on the morning of the 20th Del. at about five minutes to eight o'clock it cante on from the eastetly direction, with a roaring noise, and lasted for six seconds. Most of the inhabitants left their houses, and were to be seen standing in the centre of the streets. A few houses at the upper part of the town were severely injured. On Sunday, 7th Nov. at 25 minutes past 2, i>. m. a most dreadful and alai ming þÿexplo Sion occurred in this harbour, on heard the Havtien man-of-war barque Constitution, Which shattered everything in the air. The houses situated near the market place at the Croix de Bussal, in front of the sea, were affected by the shock, and the confusion in the air could have been seen three leagues off. The boats that were shortly in attendance, in quest of dead bodies, returned with several mutilated pieces of human fiame. It appeared that a party had been given on hoard this vessel on the day in question, and exclusive of (57 hands on board, ns well as 12 or Iff women that had been invited to attend the party, only five now survived, much injured. þÿ Morning Journal
